Rohingya in Rakhine State needed a special permit to travel to another township, and could go to Sittwe's hospital only in an emergency and with permission (Amnesty International 2017)
Rohingya students could not attend classes at Sittwe University from 2012, and were admitted again only in 2022 (DVB 2022)
After the violence of 2012 in Rakhine State, about 138,000 Rohingya lost their homes and came to live in camps (IRIN 2014)
In 1978 about 200,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, and almost all had gone back by the end of 1979. UNHCR acknowledged that up to 10,000 died in the camps in between (Crisp 2018, HPN)
In 1991-92 about 250,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, and 200,000 had gone back by mid-1995 (Crisp 2018, HPN)
In the six months from late August 2017, nearly 700,000 Rohingya fled to Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh. MSF estimated that at least 6,700 were killed by violence in the first month alone (MSF 2017, 2018)
From early 2024 to August 2026, 155,296 Rohingya newly arrived in Bangladesh's camps from Rakhine State (Bangladesh Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, 2026)
From February 2024 Myanmar's military forcibly recruited more than 1,000 Rohingya men and boys in Rakhine State (Human Rights Watch 2024)
Food aid in the camps comes as e-vouchers worth US$7-12 a person a month (Bangladesh Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, 2026)
Rohingya refugees cannot leave the camps to work. Even Rohingya teachers at the learning centres work as 'volunteers', paid 13,000 taka (about US$106) a month (Human Rights Watch 2025)

The camps' learning centres teach Myanmar's curriculum up to grade 8 or 9. Refugee children who came after 2017 cannot attend Bangladeshi schools, so they have no way to earn a recognised certificate (Bangladesh Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner 2026, Human Rights Watch 2025)
In 2025 only 57 students were in class 11 at the learning centres of the Cox's Bazar camps (Human Rights Watch 2025)
In June 2025 funding cuts closed thousands of learning centres in the camps, halting the schooling of about 304,000 children (Human Rights Watch 2025)
In early 2025 over 15% of children in the camps were malnourished, and children treated for severe acute malnutrition were up 27% on a year before (UNICEF 2025)
Many of the camps' shelters are at risk of landslides and flash floods (Bangladesh Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, 2026)
In August 2026, 33,514 Rohingya lived on Bhasan Char, an island in the Bay of Bengal (Bangladesh Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, 2026)
In 2025 more than 6,500 Rohingya set out by sea, and nearly 900 died or went missing: one in seven, the highest rate of any major refugee sea route in the world (UNHCR 2026)

By November 2023 just over 600 Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh had been resettled in third countries: 355 in the US, 131 in Canada, 48 in Australia and a few elsewhere (Bangladesh's home ministry, The Irrawaddy 2023)
